question: Let $f:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ be defined by $f(n)=\frac{n+1}{2}$ when $n$ is odd and $f(n)=\frac{n}{2}$ when $n$ is even. Determine whether $f$ is one-one and onto, and justify the classification completely.
explanation:
Verification of one-one property
Consider the two distinct natural numbers $1$ and $2$. Since $1$ is odd, $$f(1)=\frac{1+1}{2}=1$$ Since $2$ is even, $$f(2)=\frac{2}{2}=1$$ Thus, $$f(1)=f(2)$$ although $1\neq2$. Therefore, $f$ is not one-one.

Verification of onto property
Let $m\in\mathbb{N}$ be arbitrary. Choose the even natural number $$n=2m$$ Then, using the rule for even values of $n$, $$f(2m)=\frac{2m}{2}=m$$ Thus, every $m\in\mathbb{N}$ has a pre-image $2m\in\mathbb{N}$. Hence, every element of the co-domain occurs as an image, so $f$ is onto.

Final Result
The function $f$ is onto but not one-one.

options.A: $f$ is onto but not one-one because $f(1)=f(2)=1$, while every $m\in\mathbb{N}$ has the pre-image $2m$.
options.B: $f$ is one-one but not onto because only even natural numbers have images under $f$.
options.C: $f$ is both one-one and onto because every $m\in\mathbb{N}$ has exactly one pre-image.
options.D: $f$ is neither one-one nor onto because odd and even inputs are evaluated using different rules.
